item.title: Intelligence as Useful Structure: A Thermodynamic Perspective
item.description: arXiv:2610.14197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thermodynamic accounts of intelligence have advanced rapidly, but they do not yet resolve a prior definitional problem: what makes internal structure intelligent rather than merely ordered? This paper argues that any thermodynamic intelligence metric should include a usefulness filter. The numerator must track internal structure that is relevant to viability, prediction, and control, not merely raw information or benchmark score. Intelligence is therefore defined as the resource-bounded capacity of an adaptive system to acquire, compress, and deploy useful internal structure so as to improve prediction, control, and robustness across a range of environments. Capability and efficiency are separated. Capability is adaptive reach, A, defined over a reference distribution of environments or task families. Efficiency is acquisition efficiency, I_eff = Delta C_u / W_diss, where C_u denotes useful internal structure and W_diss physically dissipated work. Concretely, C_u is the predictive and control-relevant information that a system's internal state carries about viability-relevant environmental structure, making it a semantic rather than purely syntactic information term. I_eff is a learning or adaptation metric, not a complete scalar measure of deployed intelligence: trained systems at steady state may have Delta C_u = 0 while still exhibiting high adaptive reach. A toy numerical example with exact Landauer-referenced dissipation costs, explicit boundary conditions, temperature-normalised reporting conventions, and falsifiable comparisons against size-based and energy-only baselines are provided.
item.dc:creator: Boris Djordjevic

item.title: Autocatalytic order controls bistability in a conservative kinetic model of relational event progression
item.description: arXiv:2102.08826v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This version supersedes earlier versions and develops the three-class model of v1 into a closed, conserved network. On a relational view, the Universe is the happening of events rather than a container for them. A kinetic model gives this dynamical form: events are sorted as future, now or past; future events combine reversibly into now events; a now event meeting past events is activated and completes irreversibly into past events, which are renewed for future use. Past events thus catalyse their own production in a closed network conserving a weighted event count. We give a complete mass-action and bifurcation analysis. Conservation fixes the stoichiometry uniquely. When one past event participates in each activation, progression ignites softly at a transcritical threshold and no fold can arise, for every completion yield. When two participate cooperatively, the progressing branch folds: a past-rich attractor coexists with a past-poor state and ignition needs a finite perturbation. Cooperative order creates memory; nonequilibrium asymmetry only sets how hard it is to undo, strict one-way latching being a singular limit of hysteresis. In a partially reversible network where only renewal is reversible, two stable interior states coexist while activation and completion stay strictly one-way. The work is theoretical and does not derive time or its arrow: relational ordering and local irreversibility are assumed. As stated postulates, events are parcels of energy, the budget is conserved energy, and the activated class is the activated complex of transition-state theory. Around each cycle both the budget and the event number are conserved; at steady state the composition is stationary while energy is concentrated and dispersed locally, and whether entropy production vanishes globally is posed as a hypothesis.
item.dc:creator: Bruce M Boman

item.title: Optical and magnetic penetration depths under a modified electromagnetic coupling in charged bosonic condensates
item.description: arXiv:2605.20499v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We establish the relation between optical condensate spectral weight and static magnetic screening in a proposed effective theory of charged bosonic condensates with an additional diamagnetic coupling. Starting from an explicit Ginzburg--Landau functional, we derive both the London equation and the transverse low-frequency conductivity. At fixed condensate parameter $q^2n_s/m^\ast$, the modified coupling doubles the inverse-square magnetic screening length and the optical condensate weight, giving $\lambda_{\rm mag}=\lambda_{\rm stiff}=\lambda_L/\sqrt{2}$, where $\lambda_L^{-2}=\mu_0q^2n_s/m^\ast$. Their ratio is therefore unity in both the standard and modified local theories: it tests consistency between measurement methods but cannot distinguish the couplings. A structured comparison of published results for Nb, Pb, YBCO, MgB$_2$, and Ba(Fe,Co)$_2$As$_2$ identifies the roles of sample matching, absolute calibration, nonlocality, and spectral-weight extraction. We formulate the requirements for a discriminating absolute-response experiment and discuss a complementary single-particle spectral prediction. The analysis separates experimentally accessible consistency checks from tests requiring independent information about condensate parameters or a different observable.
